Instability was modest and narrowed with time, so the threat became increasingly localized overnight.

boundary_drivers: MCS over the upper Ohio Valley|outflow boundary intersecting a prefrontal confluence zone in Kentucky and Tennessee|cold front from Ohio into Kentucky and Tennessee|remnant MCS over western North Carolina

Upscale growth was expected but remained uncertain in timing.

boundary_drivers: trailing outflow boundary from weakening Michigan MCS|cold front across the Midwest|central High Plains post-frontal upslope flow|lower Colorado River Valley moisture plume
storm_modes: supercells near outflow|clusters|line segments|High Plains supercells

boundary_drivers: outflow from a decayed overnight MCS over Ohio and Kentucky|cold front from the Great Lakes into New England|dissipating front over the central High Plains|differential heating zones from Kansas to the lower Ohio Valley
storm_modes: outflow-driven clusters|bowing line segments|High Plains supercells|multicells

Damaging winds and hail dominated, while the central High Plains had a separate hail and wind risk. The eastern Enhanced corridor was strongly tied to prior-convection boundaries and recovery.

boundary_drivers: northern Plains moisture axis and lee trough|central Plains dryline/lee trough segment|eastern Carolinas frontal wave and outflow boundary|northward retreating Midwest surface ridge
storm_modes: northern Plains supercells|central Plains clusters|nocturnal MCS|Carolinas storm cluster

boundary_drivers: northern High Plains forcing in the exit region of a midlevel speed max|surface trough and cold front over Montana and the Dakotas|western Dakotas instability axis|central High Plains upslope zone
storm_modes: discrete supercells|numerous thunderstorm clusters|MCS spreading east|bowing segments
day_narrative: Numerous storms spread from eastern Montana into the Dakotas as large-scale ascent overspread the northern High Plains. Early discrete supercells transitioned toward clusters and an eastward-moving MCS, with damaging winds and large hail the main hazards. The severe risk was primarily synoptic/frontal.

boundary_drivers: well-organized line over lower Michigan|advancing cold front from Wisconsin to Ohio|trailing outflow over central lower Michigan|instability corridor from Nebraska to northern Illinois
storm_modes: organized squall line|cold-pool surge|bowing QLCS|isolated storms along front

boundary_drivers: amplifying shortwave trough from Montana into the Dakotas|cold front and surface wave across the Upper Midwest|instability axis into the lower Missouri Valley|southern-stream impulse over eastern Oklahoma
storm_modes: initial supercells|MCS with embedded bowing/LEWP structures|clusters|QLCS
day_narrative: A broad severe swath stretched from Minnesota to northeast Kansas and northwest Missouri. Initial supercells with hail and tornado potential were expected to grow upscale into an MCS with destructive wind potential. A separate weaker southern MCS corridor extended into the Mid-South.

boundary_drivers: Kansas cold front and surface trough|dryline-like western Kansas boundary|central Plains instability axis|Southeast moist multicell corridor
day_narrative: Central and eastern Kansas had the main severe risk, with cellular storms producing very large hail and localized severe winds before merging into larger clusters. Western Missouri was the downstream target later in the evening. The Carolinas and Georgia had a separate low-end moist multicell wind threat.

boundary_drivers: deepening surface cyclone from Kansas into Iowa|stalled front into central Iowa|remnant lee trough/dryline across Missouri and Arkansas|cold front across the lower Missouri Valley
storm_modes: arcing band with embedded supercells|semi-discrete supercells|QLCS segments|broken line
day_narrative: A strong fall cyclone supported a fast-moving severe band from Iowa and Missouri into Illinois. Embedded supercell structures in an arcing band produced a time-limited tornado threat, while damaging winds became increasingly dominant downstream. Moisture and instability were marginal in some corridors, limiting hail and tornado longevity.

boundary_drivers: central High Plains moisture plume|cold front pushing into Kansas and Texas|strong midlevel cooling and upper low|evening low-level jet
storm_modes: long-lived discrete supercells|cyclic supercells|developing squall line|embedded circulations
day_narrative: A late-season central High Plains event featured discrete supercells with a significant tornado threat during the evening. As the cold front advanced, storms rapidly evolved into a squall line with damaging winds and a few tornadoes. The day was a classic discrete-to-linear transition under a powerful upper system.

boundary_drivers: prefrontal squall line from Arkansas to the upper Texas coast|Pacific front advancing into the lower Mississippi Valley|strong southerly low-level jet|Gulf moisture return
storm_modes: prefrontal squall line|QLCS with embedded circulations|semi-discrete cells|overnight weakening line

Instability and organization gradually waned overnight but the line remained locally severe.

boundary_drivers: negatively tilted trough and deep surface low|prefrontal warm sector from Mississippi and Alabama into Tennessee|trailing cold front|50+ kt southerly low-level jet
storm_modes: discrete supercells|fast-moving line segments|bowing QLCS|embedded circulations

The greatest risk for strong tornadoes focused from northeast Mississippi and northern Alabama into middle Tennessee, where discrete storms could persist ahead of the main line. Damaging winds and isolated hail accompanied the broader fast-moving convective band.

boundary_drivers: cold front advancing into north and central Texas|warm sector across north Texas and southeast Oklahoma|discrete cells near the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex|Ozarks warm frontal zone
storm_modes: discrete tornadic supercells|front-parallel line|clusters|overnight elevated storms
day_narrative: North Texas and nearby Oklahoma had a focused tornado threat as discrete cells formed ahead of the advancing cold front, including near the Dallas-Fort Worth area. Hail and damaging wind also accompanied storms along and behind the boundary, with the severe risk extending into the Ozarks overnight. Cold-frontal undercutting increasingly complicated storm mode with time.

boundary_drivers: surface low moving across the Ark-La-Tex|cold front advancing from east Texas into Louisiana and Mississippi|prefrontal confluence zones across the warm sector|70 F dewpoint warm sector
day_narrative: A southern Plains upper low and Ark-La-Tex surface low drove another severe day from east Texas into Louisiana, Arkansas, Mississippi, and western Tennessee. Prefrontal cells and a broken line produced tornadoes and damaging winds, including potential for a strong tornado or two. The event gradually became more QLCS-dominant overnight.

boundary_drivers: low-level warm advection|near-coastal warm front|Pacific cold front/dryline intersection late
day_narrative: A southern-stream trough and strengthening jet supported mostly elevated supercells from southeast Texas into Louisiana during the evening and overnight. Very cold midlevels and steep lapse rates made large to significant hail the main hazard, while the tornado risk was conditional and focused near the immediate coast and warm front. Later activity also interacted with a cold front/dryline intersection, but outflow was not the controlling regime.

boundary_drivers: deepening surface cyclone|warm front|cold front|pre-frontal confluence
day_narrative: A deepening Gulf Coast cyclone moved a modest but sufficient warm sector inland across Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and the Florida Panhandle. Discrete or semi-discrete storms initially carried tornado and hail risk, then a fast-moving line near the cold front carried wind and brief tornado potential overnight. The limited moisture made destabilization and the degree of surface-based inflow important forecast concerns.

boundary_drivers: cold front|warm-sector confluence|warm front over Tennessee/Kentucky
day_narrative: A strongly forced cool-season system produced a mixed tornado and damaging-wind event from the lower Mississippi Valley into Alabama and Tennessee. The main southern warm-sector corridor supported tornadoes, including a couple strong tornadoes, while the northern part of the system evolved into a weakening but still hazardous squall line. Timing and the northward extent of surface-based instability remained key uncertainties.

boundary_drivers: deepening Gulf Coast low|warm front|pre-frontal warm sector|cold front
day_narrative: A potent Gulf Coast cyclone produced a significant tornado episode from southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi into Alabama and the western Florida Panhandle. Supercells in the moistening warm sector were the central concern, with damaging winds and isolated hail accompanying the broader convective field. The event retained some mixed-mode character, but the strongest signal was for tornadic supercells in the high-shear Gulf Coast corridor.

boundary_drivers: pre-frontal convergence axis|warm front|cold front|Appalachian lee trough
day_narrative: The prior Gulf system continued into the Carolinas and Mid-Atlantic with a broken band of storms containing embedded supercells and bowing segments. The greatest tornado threat evolved across the Carolinas into Virginia and Maryland, with a few strong tornadoes possible before the mode became more linear farther north. The event was a classic high-shear, modest-instability mixed-mode outbreak.

boundary_drivers: slow-moving upper low|dryline|convective clusters|low-level jet
day_narrative: A slow southern Plains upper low produced repeated convective clusters from Texas into Louisiana and the ArkLaTex. The ENH risk leaned on clustered and linear convection with strong shear but only marginal instability, so damaging winds and a few tornadoes were tied to convective organization more than pristine discrete initiation. The day was strongly modulated by ongoing storms and their ability to persist or redevelop overnight.

boundary_drivers: shortwave trough|warm front|Arkansas warm sector
day_narrative: Discrete supercells developed from eastern Oklahoma into Arkansas and later the lower Mississippi Valley. Very large hail was a major early threat, while increasing low-level shear raised tornado potential as storms moved into Arkansas and northern Mississippi. The event gradually became less organized with time, but the ENH signal was a supercell hail and tornado day.

boundary_drivers: deep surface low|warm front|cold front|negatively tilting shortwave
day_narrative: A vigorous Midwest cyclone supported severe supercells across Missouri, Iowa, Illinois, and adjacent areas. Central and northern Illinois became the main evening focus for tornadoes and very large hail, with storms eventually weakening or becoming more linear overnight. The cool-season shear and frontal structure made the boundary-relative storm track important.

boundary_drivers: weak baroclinic zone|persistent convection|Gulf Coast instability gradient
day_narrative: Severe hail clusters persisted from northeast Texas into Louisiana and Arkansas, while additional storms developed along a weak Gulf Coast baroclinic zone. The primary hazard was large hail, with localized wind and brief tornado potential in stronger or more surface-based cells. Convective coverage and boundary placement were more important than a clean synoptic frontal setup.

boundary_drivers: dryline|weak cold front|warm front|gravity wave/bore|pre-frontal confluence
day_narrative: A broad Plains-to-ArkLaMiss risk involved several severe regimes at once. Dryline and frontal storms over Oklahoma, Kansas, and Texas produced large hail and wind, while a more tornadic pre-frontal/warm-sector corridor evolved from northeast Texas into Arkansas and the lower Mississippi Valley overnight. Early elevated convection and convective interference made the storm mode messy and lowered confidence in any one corridor.

boundary_drivers: cold front|warm-sector confluence|ongoing convective complex|Gulf Coast warm sector
day_narrative: The second day of the late-March system produced numerous storms across Mississippi, Alabama, Tennessee, and Georgia. Strong shear supported supercells and tornadoes, but storms frequently merged into complexes and line segments, increasing the damaging-wind component. Prior convection and ongoing precipitation affected instability and the ability of discrete storms to persist.

boundary_drivers: dryline|cold front|midlevel convection|southern Plains shortwave
day_narrative: Severe storms developed from Texas into Oklahoma, southeast Kansas, and Missouri as a dryline/cold-front setup interacted with midlevel convection. Large hail was the main concern, with damaging winds and a conditional tornado risk where surface-based storms could sustain. Forecast confidence was reduced by ongoing convection and uncertainty about how quickly dryline storms would organize.

boundary_drivers: weakening southern-stream vort max|dryline|outflow boundaries|north Texas instability axis
day_narrative: A messy southern Plains to lower Mississippi Valley severe episode featured scattered storms in multiple corridors. North Texas and southeast Oklahoma carried the most organized hail and wind threat, with tornado potential conditional on storm mode and boundary interaction. The day depended heavily on how previous convection and outflow altered the warm sector.

boundary_drivers: High Plains lee trough|upslope flow|dryline|Florida sea-breeze/peninsula convergence

day_narrative: Several shortwaves ejecting into the High Plains supported supercells from eastern Colorado and western Kansas into the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. The primary ENH character was a High Plains upslope/dryline supercell day.

boundary_drivers: sharpening dryline/lee trough|weak surface low|low-level jet
day_narrative: A sharpening Plains dryline and lee trough focused late-day storms from the Missouri Valley into Kansas and Oklahoma. The main concern was supercells with large to very large hail, damaging gusts, and a couple tornadoes, especially where storms could remain discrete. Coverage was conditional because forcing was modest and capping remained important.

boundary_drivers: dryline|cold front|morning MCS/outflow|surface low
day_narrative: The day began with an MCS over the lower Missouri Valley and evolved into a central/southern Plains all-hazards event. Dryline storms initially posed very large hail and tornado risk, but upscale growth produced an elongated squall line with common damaging wind and hail from Kansas into Oklahoma and Texas. Prior convection and outflow made the transition from discrete supercells to QLCS a central forecast issue.

boundary_drivers: surface cyclone|dryline|morning elevated storms|ArkLaTex warm sector
day_narrative: A southern Plains shortwave and surface cyclone produced widespread severe potential from Texas and Oklahoma into the ArkLaTex and lower Mississippi Valley. Supercells near the dryline and warm sector carried all hazards, while earlier elevated storms and later bands complicated the spatial focus. The day was a broad, multi-mode setup rather than a single clean corridor.

boundary_drivers: surface dryline/frontal boundary|central Plains warm front|western U.S. trough
day_narrative: A western U.S. trough and Plains dryline/frontal boundary supported discrete supercells from central Kansas into western Oklahoma. The primary threats were very large hail and tornadoes, including potential for a couple strong tornadoes, before storms clustered later in the evening. The forecast depended on initiation timing and how quickly discrete cells would merge.

boundary_drivers: old outflow/differential heating zone|dryline|warm sector over southeast Oklahoma and Arkansas
day_narrative: Severe storms focused from southeast Oklahoma into Arkansas and northeast Texas along an old outflow and differential-heating boundary. Very large hail and tornadoes were the main hazards where supercells could remain organized in a highly unstable air mass. Farther north, a band of storms from Nebraska into Oklahoma produced hail and wind but gradually weakened with evening stabilization.

boundary_drivers: HP supercell outflow|Ohio Valley boundary|Texas dryline/triple point|northern Plains boundary
day_narrative: This was a multi-region severe day, with the ENH risk in the Ohio Valley and other severe areas in Texas and the northern Plains. An HP supercell near the Ohio River produced very large hail, damaging winds, and possible tornado risk, while its outflow limited severe potential nearby. Texas storms carried a large-hail and wind threat along the dryline, reinforcing the mixed nature of the day.

boundary_drivers: remnant boundary in southern Illinois|southwest-moving outflow across Missouri|Texas triple point|dryline
day_narrative: Severe storms were expected from north Texas and Oklahoma into the Missouri and mid-Mississippi Valleys, with hail and wind dominant. The most important mesoscale features were remnant and outflow boundaries left by earlier convection, especially across Missouri, Illinois, and nearby areas. Additional storms near the Texas triple point added another dryline/frontal component to the day.

boundary_drivers: southward-moving cold front|High Plains shortwave|dryline in southwest Texas
day_narrative: Storms formed along a southward-moving front in the Texas/Oklahoma Panhandles and moved into western Oklahoma. Large hail was a key early hazard, but the event transitioned into a bowing complex with 70-80 mph wind potential. Southwest Texas dryline storms were a secondary severe area with isolated hail and wind.

boundary_drivers: southward-moving boundary|central Texas cold front|Rio Grande/Edwards Plateau instability gradient
day_narrative: A southward-moving boundary and subtle shortwave focused severe clusters across southwest and south-central Texas. Supercell structures produced large hail and damaging winds, with a brief tornado possible in the strongest storms. The event was more boundary-driven and clustered than a clean dryline supercell setup.

boundary_drivers: northward-moving front|effective front/convective outflow|South Texas moisture axis|northwest Gulf QLCS
day_narrative: Severe storms developed from south-central and southeast Texas into southwest Louisiana as a boundary lifted north and interacted with elevated convection. Later, a vigorous QLCS over the northwest Gulf moved ashore with wind and mesovortex potential along the effective front. This was a strongly outflow/effective-boundary modulated day rather than a simple synoptic-front event.

boundary_drivers: north-south dryline|High Plains upslope flow|lee trough|shortwave trough
day_narrative: A broad Great Plains severe day featured dryline and upslope supercells from the southern High Plains into Nebraska and South Dakota. Strong instability and adequate shear favored very large hail, damaging winds, and a few tornadoes. Coverage and longevity varied by corridor, but the core mode was discrete to semi-discrete supercells along the dryline and High Plains boundaries.

boundary_drivers: retreating dryline|large-scale outflow boundary|west Texas instability corridor
day_narrative: Scattered severe supercells developed from west Texas into western Oklahoma along a retreating dryline and nearby outflow boundary. Very large hail was the primary hazard, with tornado potential increasing during the evening where backed flow and boundary interactions improved low-level shear. The day was conditionally significant but dependent on sustaining storms along the dryline/outflow intersection.

boundary_drivers: dryline|residual outflow boundaries|central High Plains boundary|northwest Oklahoma instability axis
storm_modes: tornadic supercells|long-lived supercell cluster|MCS on southern/eastern flank
day_narrative: This was a high-end boundary-interaction supercell day from southwest Kansas and northwest Oklahoma into the Texas Panhandle. Residual outflow and the dryline focused intense supercells, including tornadic storms, with very large hail and damaging winds also likely. Later convection on the southern/eastern periphery of an MCS added a secondary clustered hazard area.

boundary_drivers: deepening southwest Kansas low|warm front|dryline|large-scale outflow boundaries
day_narrative: A very unstable central/southern Plains warm sector supported a MDT risk for supercells with strong tornadoes and very large hail from Kansas into Oklahoma and west Texas. The environment was unusually favorable, but ongoing convection and residual outflow boundaries made storm evolution messy and eventually favored multiple MCS/QLCS structures. Boundary interactions remained central through the evening, including near the warm front and dryline/outflow intersections.

boundary_drivers: lee trough|post-MCS instability gradient|southwest Texas boundary|High Plains upslope flow
day_narrative: Prior overnight MCSs substantially modified the southern Plains warm sector, leaving the best severe potential in southwest Texas and parts of the western High Plains. Isolated to widely scattered storms still posed large hail, damaging wind, and a couple tornadoes where stronger instability remained. The day had a strong recovery and coverage uncertainty component.

boundary_drivers: warm front lifting into New Jersey/New York|upper trough|pre-existing convective clusters
day_narrative: A broad eastern U.S. severe day produced multiple clusters from the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast southward into Georgia. The ENH area expanded near New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and New York as a warm front lifted north and stronger flow supported organized wind-producing storms. Supercells were possible, but damaging wind from clusters and line segments was the primary hazard.

boundary_drivers: frontal boundary from North Dakota into Montana|upslope flow north of the front|northern Rockies impulse
day_narrative: Scattered supercells developed across central and eastern Montana into the Dakotas within an upslope/frontal regime. Large to very large hail was the main hazard, with damaging wind and a tornado or two also possible. Additional marginal severe areas existed, but the primary ENH character was northern High Plains supercells.

boundary_drivers: Upper Midwest frontal zone|warm front|Montana boundary|low-level jet
day_narrative: Severe storms affected the Upper Midwest while another organized severe area developed across Montana. Minnesota and Wisconsin had the main wind/hail threat with some tornado potential, while Montana storms included supercells capable of very large hail. The day combined multiple corridors and storm modes rather than one dominant boundary type.

boundary_drivers: eastern Montana instability axis|leading edge of convection|northern High Plains shortwave
day_narrative: Eastern Montana and western North Dakota were the focus for severe storms in a steep-lapse-rate High Plains environment. The initial supercell/hail threat evolved into an arcing line and clusters with damaging wind potential, while one or two tornadoes remained possible. The ENH day was mainly a High Plains supercell-to-cluster evolution.

boundary_drivers: southward-moving MCS outflow|augmented synoptic boundary|High Plains upslope|dryline/trough
day_narrative: The central High Plains severe risk was strongly shaped by outflow from a southward-moving MCS, which enhanced the synoptic boundary across eastern Colorado, southwest Kansas, and the Panhandles. Supercells and clusters produced large hail, damaging wind, and a few tornadoes. Farther north, additional High Plains storms added a broader wind/hail component.

boundary_drivers: Upper Midwest warm front|Pacific front|dryline|decaying outflow/differential heating in OK/TX
day_narrative: The Upper Midwest warm front supported organized storms and possible mini supercells, while the central and southern Plains risk remained highly conditional. Backed low-level flow near the warm front supported a localized tornado threat, with hail and wind more broadly possible. Weak forcing and capping made the southern Plains dryline/outflow corridor uncertain.

boundary_drivers: Appalachian/Mid-Atlantic upper trough|linear convective system|cold front|northern Plains instability axis
day_narrative: A linear convective system crossed the central Appalachians into the Mid-Atlantic, producing an enhanced wind-damage threat in Virginia and nearby areas. Embedded circulations and discrete storms allowed a tornado or two, but damaging wind was the main hazard. A separate northern Plains severe area carried more isolated hail/wind/tornado potential.

boundary_drivers: northwest flow aloft|surface cold front|storm-scale cold pools|moist Southeast air mass
day_narrative: A northwest-flow regime and cold front supported organized severe multicell clusters across the Gulf Coast and Southeast. The main hazard was damaging wind, with swaths of wind damage focused where clusters bowed and accelerated. Other severe corridors existed in the Plains and Upper Midwest, but the Southeast wind event defined the ENH day.

boundary_drivers: northern Montana/ND instability corridor|warm front/baroclinic zone|storm-cluster cold pool
day_narrative: Northern Montana into North Dakota was the main severe corridor, with supercells capable of large hail and a tornado threat during the evening. As storms grew upscale, the hazard transitioned toward a swath of damaging wind with embedded hail overnight. The day was a High Plains supercell-to-MCS transition.

boundary_drivers: fast-moving northern-stream shortwave|Minnesota frontal zone|upper Great Lakes instability corridor
day_narrative: Scattered severe storms developed across Minnesota and moved toward northwest Wisconsin and western Upper Michigan. Supercells were capable of large hail, damaging winds, and a couple tornadoes, while other areas remained limited by capping and sparse coverage. The event was primarily a frontal/shortwave supercell and cluster day.

boundary_drivers: northern Plains surface low|frontal boundary|low-level jet|Mid-Atlantic lee trough
day_narrative: Severe storms were forecast across the northern Plains during the evening and then into the mid-Missouri and mid-Mississippi Valleys overnight. Large hail and damaging winds were the main hazards as storms organized in a strong instability and low-level jet regime. A separate Mid-Atlantic severe area produced localized wind and hail earlier in the day.

boundary_drivers: evolving severe storm cluster|warm front|Lake Michigan/Illinois boundary zone|storm-scale cold pool
day_narrative: A high-impact MCS evolved across northern Illinois and moved into Indiana, Michigan, and Ohio with widespread damaging winds. Embedded rotations and supercells near the warm frontal zone maintained a tornado threat, including strong tornado concern early in the evening. The MDT classification is best described as a derecho/QLCS wind event with embedded tornado and hail hazards.

boundary_drivers: pre-frontal wind shift|west-east convective band|High Plains boundaries|Ozarks instability axis
day_narrative: The day featured multiple severe corridors from Kentucky/Tennessee to the Carolinas, the Ozarks, and the High Plains. Bowing structures in a west-east band produced a damaging-wind threat, while other clusters and supercells produced hail and isolated tornado potential. The result was a messy multi-region, multi-mode ENH day.

boundary_drivers: Upper Great Lakes cold front|strong midlevel jet|trailing frontal zone into the Plains
day_narrative: A line of strong to severe storms crossed northern Wisconsin and western Upper Michigan with damaging winds as the primary threat. Strong midlevel flow along the Upper Great Lakes cold front supported organized linear convection, while additional storms developed farther southwest along the trailing front. The ENH risk was mainly a QLCS wind episode.

boundary_drivers: forward-propagating MCS|cold pool|High Plains instability axis|northwest-flow steering
day_narrative: A forward-propagating MCS evolved across the central High Plains, producing a likelihood of widespread damaging winds from northeast Colorado and western Nebraska into Kansas. Earlier supercells and clusters quickly grew upscale into a mature wind-producing system. This was one of the clearest 2016 examples of an MCS-driven MDT wind day.

boundary_drivers: northwest-flow storm track|central High Plains instability axis|storm-generated cold pool
day_narrative: A northwest-flow pattern supported widely spaced storm clusters moving southeast across the central and northern High Plains. The main ENH concern evolved into a small forward-propagating MCS over Nebraska with severe wind gusts and hail. A drier boundary layer compared to the previous day limited the magnitude but did not eliminate organized wind risk.

boundary_drivers: Northeast upper trough|surface cold front|Appalachian/Mid-Atlantic pre-frontal corridor
day_narrative: Severe storms developed across the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic with supercells in eastern New York and later linear organization closer to the coastal corridor. Damaging wind, hail, and a brief tornado or two were possible, with the strongest wind risk tied to line/QLCS evolution. A separate central Plains area remained more isolated.

boundary_drivers: warm-advection zone|effective boundary|developing thunderstorm clusters|elevated mixed-layer nose
day_narrative: One or two thunderstorm clusters were expected to grow upscale across the Upper Midwest and middle Missouri Valley into the central Plains. The main hazard was potentially damaging wind, with hail and isolated tornadoes accompanying early or embedded supercells. The forecast hinged on MCS development and how clusters interacted with the effective boundary overnight.

boundary_drivers: bowing MCSs over SD/NE|storm-scale cold pools|Red River storm cluster|Southeast remnant MCS
storm_modes: vigorous bowing segments|linear storm clusters|long-lived MCS
day_narrative: Several thunderstorm complexes produced a major damaging-wind threat from South Dakota and Nebraska into adjacent states. The MDT area emphasized intense wind gusts with vigorous bowing segments, while additional long-lived MCS activity affected the southern Appalachians and a storm cluster moved along the Red River. The event was dominated by MCS mode and cold-pool evolution.

boundary_drivers: large bowing line in Missouri/Illinois|Lower Ohio Valley instability corridor|Mid/Lower Missouri Valley boundary
day_narrative: The day had two ENH corridors: a damaging-wind MCS/squall-line risk across Kentucky and Tennessee, and a developing severe threat across the lower to mid-Missouri Valley. Damaging winds were the primary hazard, but hail and isolated tornadoes were possible with stronger storms. Prior convection and ongoing bowing segments heavily influenced the eastern corridor.

boundary_drivers: MCV from overnight convection|effective front/outflow in Oklahoma|Appalachian instability corridor
day_narrative: An MCV and associated convective cluster moved from the Ohio Valley toward the Appalachians, supporting a focused wind and hail threat from Kentucky and West Virginia into Virginia and North Carolina. In Oklahoma, an effective front marked by outflow provided another severe focus. The day was classic MCV/outflow reintensification with damaging wind as the dominant hazard.

boundary_drivers: North Dakota/SD instability axis|strengthening low-level jet|surface cyclone/frontal zone
day_narrative: A severe line/MCS crossed North Dakota into South Dakota and western Minnesota during the evening. Damaging wind and large hail were the primary hazards, with activity building southward into extreme instability and a strengthening low-level jet. The day was primarily a northern Plains MCS wind/hail event.

boundary_drivers: outflow boundary across Minnesota/South Dakota|warm front|weak MCVs over the Mid-South|secondary surface low
day_narrative: Severe potential extended from the Upper Midwest into the Plains, with the most important mesoscale tornado signal near an outflow boundary in Minnesota and South Dakota. Storms interacting with that boundary and a nearby warm front could produce localized tornadoes, hail, and wind, while a bowing segment in Wisconsin raised wind risk. Farther south, weak MCVs and prior convective overturning limited and focused the Southeast threat.

boundary_drivers: merging High Plains storm clusters|forward-propagating cold pool|western Oklahoma/Texas Panhandle instability corridor
day_narrative: Storm clusters from Colorado and Kansas merged and moved south-southeast toward western Oklahoma and the Texas Panhandle. Initial storms could produce very large hail and a brief tornado, but the main overnight ENH hazard was damaging wind from a forward-propagating MCS. The event depended on how quickly upscale growth occurred.

boundary_drivers: leading edge of northern Plains convection|warm-sector instability|shortwave over the northern High Plains
day_narrative: Northern and central Plains storms formed along the leading edge of convection and spread eastward toward the Upper Mississippi Valley. Large hail and damaging wind were the main hazards, with severe clusters merging into a broader MCS over South Dakota and Minnesota. The event was a warm-season MCS transition from initial clusters.

boundary_drivers: northern Plains theta-e axis|surface frontal zone|Iowa instability corridor|Northeast shortwave
day_narrative: A northern Plains severe corridor overlapped a separate Iowa and Northeast severe threat. The main ENH risk was large hail, damaging wind, and possibly a couple tornadoes with storms over the Dakotas and adjacent areas, while Iowa and Maine had more localized severe potential. The day was multi-region and mixed-mode, with outflow/MCS influence secondary to synoptic and thermodynamic boundaries.

boundary_drivers: multiple ongoing convective clusters|cloud/precipitation shield|Upper Mississippi Valley instability recovery|effective boundaries
day_narrative: The Upper Mississippi Valley severe risk was dominated by ongoing convective clusters, cloud cover, and differential recovery. The ENH area depended on destabilization west of earlier precipitation and renewed storms developing on effective boundaries. Damaging wind and large hail were the main hazards, with additional severe areas from New England to the Mid-South.

boundary_drivers: Finger Lakes storm outflow|Northeast/Mid-Atlantic instability corridor|midlevel flow over PA/NJ/NY
day_narrative: The ENH upgrade across Pennsylvania, southeast New York, and New Jersey was for damaging wind from organized thunderstorms in a moderately to strongly unstable air mass. Ongoing storms near the Finger Lakes and development along their outflow were important to the corridor. Hail was secondary, and the main question was how concentrated the wind swath would become.

boundary_drivers: central High Plains boundary|ongoing southwest Nebraska MCS|Kansas instability corridor|Mid-Atlantic boundaries
day_narrative: Central High Plains storms initially posed large hail and a couple tornadoes from eastern Colorado into Kansas and northern Oklahoma. The key evolution was upscale growth into an MCS/squall line with damaging wind potential as it moved southeast into more unstable air. The day was a mixed discrete-to-linear High Plains severe episode.

boundary_drivers: northern Plains frontal zone|midlevel closed low/trough|North Dakota to northwest Minnesota instability axis
day_narrative: Severe storms developed across the eastern Dakotas into northwest Minnesota as forcing increased downstream of a midlevel low. A supercell in North Dakota produced tornado concern, while additional storms grew upscale with damaging wind and hail risk into the night. The event was a northern Plains supercell-to-cluster transition.

boundary_drivers: central Rockies impulse|central/northern Plains lee/frontal boundary|South Dakota/Nebraska instability corridor
day_narrative: An impulse from the central Rockies supported scattered severe storms over South Dakota and Nebraska. Initial discrete supercells posed hail, wind, and a tornado threat, but storms were expected to merge into lines and clusters with a more concentrated damaging-wind risk. The day was a High Plains to central Plains supercell-to-line transition.

boundary_drivers: cold front from Nebraska into Kansas|Oklahoma dryline|strong shortwave trough|conditional central/southern Oklahoma forcing
day_narrative: A strong fall shortwave and Plains cold front/dryline supported severe storms from Oklahoma into Kansas, Nebraska, and adjacent areas. Very large hail and tornadoes were possible with supercells, including a conditional but potentially intense Oklahoma corridor. Storm coverage and forcing in central/southern Oklahoma were key uncertainties.

boundary_drivers: accelerating shortwave|cold front|dryline|pre-existing thunderstorm/cloud shield|warm-sector recovery
day_narrative: A strong shortwave and cold front/dryline produced severe storms from Kansas and Nebraska into Iowa and Missouri, with a conditional Oklahoma/Texas dryline area. Tornado probabilities increased across eastern Kansas and nearby areas, including potential for a strong tornado or two before storms became more linear. Prior clouds and storms complicated warm-sector recovery but did not dominate the setup.

boundary_drivers: deep occluded cyclone|ejecting shortwave|lower Mississippi Valley warm sector|squall line
day_narrative: A large Plains cyclone and ejecting southern-stream shortwave supported severe storms from Louisiana into Mississippi and the Tennessee Valley. Semi-discrete storms produced tornado potential, while a squall line later carried damaging-wind and embedded tornado risk. Instability was modest and the severe corridor depended on warm-sector quality and storm mode.

boundary_drivers: lifting warm front|moist Gulf warm sector|low-level jet|pre-frontal confluence
day_narrative: A significant late-season Dixie Alley tornado outbreak unfolded from Louisiana and Mississippi into northern Alabama and southern Tennessee. Classic supercells developed near a lifting warm front in a strongly sheared moist warm sector, with damaging wind also persisting overnight. Some early elevated convection and questions about downstream sustainability existed, but the main character was high-end tornadic supercells.

boundary_drivers: strong cold front|ArkLaMiss warm sector|central Appalachian frontal corridor
day_narrative: A late-season frontal system produced severe storms from the ArkLaMiss and Mid-South into the central Appalachians. Damaging wind was the primary hazard, with a few tornadoes possible in semi-discrete cells ahead of the cold front and embedded circulations in the line. The threat gradually weakened overnight as instability diminished and low-topped convection moved east.

boundary_drivers: eastward-moving cold front|coastal warm front|pre-frontal confluence bands
day_narrative: A compact southern-stream wave drove a Gulf Coast severe episode with an eastward-moving bowing line and discrete storms in the warm sector. The main corridor shifted from Louisiana and Mississippi toward Alabama, Georgia, and the Florida Panhandle as convection regulated the warm front and instability.

boundary_drivers: weak Gulf Coast warm front|low-level warm advection|developing low-level jet
storm_modes: elevated supercells|discrete to semi-discrete storms|overnight bowing complex
day_narrative: Initial storms developed near the Texas coast and spread into Louisiana with a large to very large hail threat. Overnight, the environment became more favorable for tornadoes and damaging winds as convection expanded eastward along the warm front and low-level jet.

boundary_drivers: northward-moving warm front|outflow from morning convection|approaching cold front
day_narrative: This was the first major day of the late-January Southeast outbreak, with multiple rounds from Louisiana and Arkansas into Georgia and the Carolinas. Discrete supercells and larger clusters produced a full-spectrum severe threat, with the late-day and overnight risk focused near the warm front and recovering outflow zones.

boundary_drivers: warm front near south Georgia/north Florida|pre-frontal convergence|outflow/warm-frontal corridor
day_narrative: A HIGH risk was issued for a Southeast tornado outbreak centered on north Florida and south Georgia, later extending into the Carolinas and Florida Peninsula. The day featured tornadic supercells and broken lines within a strongly sheared warm sector, then a later southward shift as the main threat focused over Florida.

boundary_drivers: warm front lifting into MS/AL|cold front|southern flank of ongoing clusters
day_narrative: Widespread convection across Louisiana and Mississippi constrained destabilization but still supported a corridor of severe storms along its southern edge. The dominant threat was damaging wind with a few tornadoes as clusters and a squall line advanced into the central Gulf Coast states.

boundary_drivers: organizing convective complex|surface low track|southeast Texas to western Louisiana corridor
storm_modes: quasi-linear convective system|line segments|conditional overnight convection
day_narrative: A morning QLCS crossed southeast Texas toward the Sabine River with damaging wind and a few tornadoes. SPC noted a relative lull after the initial system, then only conditional overnight severe potential across the central Gulf Coast.

boundary_drivers: advancing cold front|pre-frontal confluence axis|warm front near lower Michigan
storm_modes: broken bands|linear segments|rotating updrafts within bands
day_narrative: Severe storms formed in bands from southeast Lower Michigan southward into Kentucky and Tennessee. The primary threat was damaging wind, with hail and a tornado or two possible as stronger updrafts rotated within the bands.

boundary_drivers: cold front|warm front|pre-existing boundary/vorticity zones
day_narrative: A widespread severe episode developed from the lower Mississippi Valley to the Ohio Valley, with strong tornado potential focused from southern Missouri into the middle Ohio Valley. Supercells were favored initially, with damaging wind and hail continuing as storms increased in coverage overnight.

boundary_drivers: cold front|MCV within morning squall line|trailing convective outflow
day_narrative: The day began with a mature squall line and MCV over the Ohio and Tennessee Valleys, supporting a MDT for widespread wind damage. As the system moved east into the Appalachians and Mid-Atlantic, damaging wind remained dominant with embedded tornado potential and renewed storms farther south.

boundary_drivers: dryline|overtaking cold front|warm front tied to deepening surface low
day_narrative: A deepening northern Plains cyclone and trailing dryline/cold front supported severe storms from the Plains into the Mississippi Valley. Initial supercells posed tornado and very large hail risk, then the dominant hazard shifted toward damaging wind as a QLCS matured overnight.

boundary_drivers: cold pool mergers|instability axis|cold front/dryline zone
day_narrative: Storms over the Ozark Plateau evolved from hail-producing convection into a line and MCS that moved toward the Tennessee Valley. The severe threat transitioned from large hail to damaging winds as cold pools merged and the system propagated southeastward.

boundary_drivers: weak frontal boundary|progressive shortwave trough|instability gradient into the Tennessee Valley
day_narrative: A thunderstorm cluster over Tennessee intensified into a forward-propagating MCS, producing a concentrated severe-wind corridor into northern Alabama, Georgia, and the Carolinas. Hail accompanied the stronger storms, but wind damage was the signature hazard.

boundary_drivers: closed cyclone over the south-central High Plains|cold front|Ark-La-Tex warm sector
day_narrative: A closed cyclone moving toward the Ozarks supported severe storms from east Texas into the Ark-La-Tex and lower Mississippi Valley. The primary threat became damaging wind with a few tornadoes as storms organized into bands and a squall line overnight.

boundary_drivers: dryline/pacific front|moisture plume into Oklahoma and north Texas|approaching shortwave trough
day_narrative: Central/eastern Oklahoma into north Texas had a focused MDT for supercells capable of very large hail, tornadoes, and damaging winds. The late evening outlook downgraded to ENH as storms evolved into clusters and the threat became more scattered.

boundary_drivers: midlevel shortwave trough|cold front|moist warm sector into KY/TN/MS/AL
day_narrative: Severe storms spread from the Lower Mississippi and Ohio Valleys into the Tennessee Valley with damaging winds and large hail as the primary threats. Tornado potential existed with stronger embedded or semi-discrete storms, but the event was mainly cluster/line driven.

boundary_drivers: dryline|upper low/shortwave trough|cold front into the southern Plains
day_narrative: The southern Plains had a MDT for numerous severe storms, with very large hail, tornadoes, and damaging winds likely. By evening, several clusters had congealed across Texas and Oklahoma, shifting the risk toward MCS wind while still retaining tornado potential.

boundary_drivers: slow-moving surface low|warm front/outflow-modified corridor|low-level jet
day_narrative: A slow-moving upper low and surface system produced multiple clusters from eastern Oklahoma and far east Texas into Missouri and the lower/middle Mississippi Valley. Tornado and damaging-wind threats were most focused where storms interacted with warm-frontal or outflow-modified zones.

boundary_drivers: sharp east-west warm front in Indiana|southern Alabama pre-MCS warm sector|coastal Carolina boundary
day_narrative: Severe potential was split between the Midwest/Ohio Valley, Alabama/Florida Panhandle, and later coastal Carolinas. Warm-front interactions in Indiana and storm clusters ahead of an approaching MCS in Alabama supported a mixed, mostly wind/tornado/hail event.

boundary_drivers: Sabine Valley to lower Mississippi Valley warm sector|squall line western edge|central Gulf Coast warm front
storm_modes: discrete tornadic supercells|PDS tornado-watch storms|squall line with QLCS tornadoes
day_narrative: A HIGH risk was introduced from east Texas into Louisiana and the lower Mississippi Valley for significant tornadoes, severe wind, and hail. Discrete storms in central Louisiana carried the strongest tornado threat before a squall line and nocturnal Gulf Coast severe-wind/tornado risk became dominant.

boundary_drivers: long-lived squall line|progressive MCS|destabilizing warm sector into Georgia/Carolinas
storm_modes: broken squall line|supercells ahead of line|embedded mesovortices
day_narrative: The previous day's system continued east with a long-lived squall line across Georgia, the Florida Panhandle, and the Carolinas. Damaging wind remained the main threat, with isolated tornadoes possible from embedded circulations and storms ahead of the line.

boundary_drivers: central Oklahoma warm sector|dryline/cold front|central Gulf Coast warm-advection zone
day_narrative: Strong forcing and an intense midlevel jet supported severe storms across Oklahoma into Missouri and Arkansas, with a later Gulf Coast hail/wind risk. Initial storms posed very large hail and tornado potential before a more linear wind threat evolved northeastward.

boundary_drivers: Southeast warm sector|warm front/coastal baroclinic zone|advancing cold front/trough
day_narrative: A HIGH risk outbreak unfolded from Alabama and Georgia into South Carolina, the Ohio Valley, and the Mid-Atlantic. The highest-end tornado potential was tied to discrete and semi-discrete storms in a strongly sheared warm sector, with very large hail and damaging winds also expected.

boundary_drivers: secondary cyclone near the Blue Ridge|pre-frontal band|residual coastal convection
day_narrative: The trailing part of the April 5 system produced a morning to early-afternoon Mid-Atlantic severe threat. Low-level moisture was somewhat disrupted by earlier convection, limiting the ceiling, but strong forcing and shear still supported damaging wind, hail, and a couple tornadoes.

boundary_drivers: surface cyclone near KS/NE|dryline/cold front|warm front into Iowa/Wisconsin
day_narrative: A central Plains to upper Mississippi Valley setup produced severe storms along a cyclone, dryline/cold front, and warm front. Hail and wind were widespread concerns, with tornado potential focused where supercells could remain organized near the frontal zones.

boundary_drivers: warm front across Lower Michigan|cold front into the southern Plains|warm-advection regime north of a shallow cool air mass
day_narrative: Severe storms occurred in two regimes: an Ohio Valley/Great Lakes wind and hail corridor, and a southern Plains elevated hail threat overnight. The day was not a classic tornado setup; damaging winds and hail dominated the risk.

boundary_drivers: morning convective system/outflow|cold front|north Texas to Arkansas warm sector
day_narrative: The day featured a morning damaging-wind MCS from Oklahoma into Arkansas, followed by later severe redevelopment from north-central Texas into Arkansas. Very large hail, damaging winds, and a few tornadoes were possible where the atmosphere recovered along the boundary network.

boundary_drivers: cold front from southeast Kansas to Oklahoma|approaching upper trough|northeast Oklahoma to western Missouri instability corridor
day_narrative: Storms increased along a cold front from Oklahoma and southeast Kansas into western Missouri and northwest Arkansas. Very large hail and damaging wind were the main threats, with a tornado or two possible early before storms became more clustered.

boundary_drivers: surging outflow boundary|approaching cold front|Lower Mississippi Valley warm sector
day_narrative: A MDT was in place across the Lower Mississippi Valley for tornadoes, hail, and damaging winds from northeast Texas into Arkansas and northern Louisiana. Later updates emphasized the surging outflow boundary and anafrontal character, lowering confidence in discrete tornado coverage while maintaining a significant severe threat.

boundary_drivers: Ohio River boundary corridor|southern Plains dryline/front|warm-advection elevated zone
day_narrative: Severe potential was split between the Ohio River corridor and the southern Plains/Ozarks. Elevated hail was important early, while the southern Plains retained conditional tornado and very large hail potential before nocturnal clusters expanded.

boundary_drivers: deepening southern Plains cyclone|frontal boundary|pre-frontal warm sector
day_narrative: The risk continued across eastern Texas into the Ozarks and lower Mississippi Valley as a deep cyclone evolved over the southern Plains. Pre-frontal supercells carried a tornado risk, while a forced squall line supported damaging winds and hail.

boundary_drivers: broken line over LA/MS|residual outflows|east/northeast-moving MCV
day_narrative: A broken line of storms that had produced pre-dawn tornadoes continued from Louisiana/Mississippi into Alabama and Tennessee. The threat was mainly damaging wind and a couple tornadoes from embedded mesovortices and bowing segments, with later recovery behind prior outflow uncertain.

boundary_drivers: cold front from OH Valley to Georgia|downslope-prefrontal warm sector|midlevel trough
day_narrative: A broad eastern U.S. cold-frontal event produced scattered to numerous severe storms from New York and Pennsylvania southward through the Virginias and Carolinas. Damaging wind and a few tornadoes were the primary concerns, with weak lapse rates limiting hail potential.

boundary_drivers: large MCS over LA/TX|outflow boundary|Gulf Coast warm sector
storm_modes: large MCS|elevated storms north of outflow|embedded/southern-edge supercells
day_narrative: A large MCS dominated the Gulf Coast severe setup, stabilizing parts of Louisiana while maintaining severe potential along and south of its outflow. Damaging winds, hail, and a couple tornadoes remained possible from east Texas across Louisiana and southern Mississippi.

boundary_drivers: eastern New Mexico/west Texas upslope flow|dryline/lee trough|outflow-modified terrain corridor
day_narrative: Eastern New Mexico and west Texas were the focus for supercells capable of tornadoes, very large hail, and damaging wind. Earlier convection and outflow lowered confidence in some areas, but the southern half of the watch retained the greatest tornado potential into evening.

boundary_drivers: trailing outflow boundary into west Texas|triple point near the Caprock|warm front into IA/IL/IN
day_narrative: A weakening morning MCS left an outflow boundary from Kansas into west Texas, focusing later supercell development near the Caprock and northwest Texas. Very large hail was the strongest signal, with tornado potential where storms remained discrete and interacted with boundaries.

boundary_drivers: diffuse surface pattern near OK/AR/KS/MO|MCV/front/outflow boundaries across KY/VA/NC|Ark-La-Tex corridor
day_narrative: A closed trough and diffuse surface pattern supported severe storms from Oklahoma and Arkansas into the Ark-La-Tex, with another corridor extending into the Appalachians and Carolinas. Very large hail and damaging wind were most widespread, while a few tornadoes were possible in stronger supercells.

boundary_drivers: warm front from Iowa to Wisconsin|High Plains lee trough|cold pool/outflow from northern Iowa MCS
day_narrative: A compact but severe MCS developed over northern Iowa and raced toward Wisconsin and northern Illinois, producing wind and hail along the warm front. Separate severe clusters occurred across the central and northern High Plains, making this a multi-region wind/hail day.

boundary_drivers: southern High Plains dryline|warm-sector capping gradient|central Plains frontal/cluster corridor
day_narrative: A broad MDT corridor extended from west Texas and the southern High Plains into the central Plains and Upper Midwest. The highest-impact signal was for discrete supercells with giant hail and tornado potential, while other clusters produced significant wind farther north.

boundary_drivers: surface low over northern Iowa|upper Mississippi Valley warm sector|band of ascent ahead of upper trough
day_narrative: Severe storms continued across the mid to upper Mississippi Valley as a negatively tilted trough and surface low moved northeast. Damaging wind became the primary hazard, especially across eastern Iowa into northwest Illinois and southwest Wisconsin, with hail and brief tornadoes also possible.

boundary_drivers: southern/central Plains dryline|warm front|later large MCS/cold pool
day_narrative: A HIGH risk was issued for a southern and central Plains outbreak with long-lived supercells, strong tornadoes, and very large hail. By evening a large MCS expanded across Oklahoma into Kansas, shifting the threat toward wind and hail while reducing parts of the initial tornado corridor.

boundary_drivers: stationary front|outflow-modified warm sector|northern Texas to southeast Oklahoma corridor
day_narrative: Severe potential extended from the central/southern Plains into the Ozarks and Ohio Valley, but the most focused corridor was northern Texas into southeastern Oklahoma. SPC noted a nebulous convective evolution, with hail, damaging wind, and some tornado threat depending on storm organization.

boundary_drivers: southern Appalachians lee/convergence zone|Carolina Piedmont destabilization corridor|convectively stabilized outflow areas
day_narrative: Severe storms developed from Florida into the Carolinas and Ohio Valley, with the highest tornado risk in the Carolina Piedmont. Earlier convection diminished the threat in some areas, leaving a focused corridor where heating, shear, and boundaries overlapped.

boundary_drivers: triple point in northeast Colorado|cold front across Nebraska/Colorado|dryline and convective inhibition gradient
day_narrative: A one-outlook ENH focused on the central High Plains as a linear cluster formed near the northeast Colorado triple point. Very steep lapse rates and organized storm structures favored severe gusts, large hail, and a brief tornado before storms weakened eastward.

boundary_drivers: outflow boundary and stalled front|dryline near I-35|cold front into northeast Oklahoma
storm_modes: multiple severe convective systems|forward-propagating MCS|discrete supercells near dryline
day_narrative: A MDT was maintained for widespread severe wind from the Ozarks toward the Tennessee Valley, while the Red River to Ozark corridor retained giant hail and tornado potential. Multiple severe convective systems and boundaries governed the day, with dryline supercells adding a separate high-end hail/tornado component.

boundary_drivers: instability gradient across northern Wisconsin|warm front|upslope regime in CO/WY secondary area
day_narrative: A mature bowing MCS moved across northern Wisconsin into Upper Michigan with a substantial damaging-wind threat. Isolated severe storms were possible in upslope flow along the Front Range, but the Great Lakes MCS was the main event.

boundary_drivers: north-central High Plains moisture/upslope corridor|bent-back front|lee trough/dryline
day_narrative: The north-central High Plains had a MDT for supercells capable of tornadoes, very large hail, and damaging winds. PDS watch language and MDs confirmed a high-end supercell environment, while separate severe corridors existed in the northern Rockies and Upper Midwest.

boundary_drivers: Upper Midwest QLCS corridor|dryline from Nebraska to west Texas|warm front/low-level jet
day_narrative: Two severe regimes emerged: an Upper Midwest QLCS and dryline supercells from Nebraska to west Texas. Damaging wind became more prominent with the QLCS, while very large hail and a few tornadoes remained possible with more discrete storms.

boundary_drivers: central Kansas into northern Oklahoma instability axis|congealing severe storms|cold-pool driven propagation
day_narrative: A MDT focused on central/southern/eastern Kansas into northern Oklahoma for widespread and potentially destructive wind. Severe storms congealed and accelerated east/southeast, with large hail also likely across a broader corridor.

boundary_drivers: merged supercell cluster over Nebraska/Iowa|cold pool/outflow-driven acceleration|southeast Nebraska to northwest Missouri corridor
day_narrative: The day was upgraded late as a robust cluster of merged supercells crossed Nebraska and western Iowa. Widespread damaging wind became possible across southeast Nebraska, Iowa, northeast Kansas, and northwest Missouri, with large hail and embedded tornado potential.

boundary_drivers: surface cold front from Wisconsin to Kansas|mid/upper shortwave trough|instability axis into southern Plains
day_narrative: Ongoing severe storms extended from the central/southern Plains to the middle Mississippi Valley and southern Lower Michigan. Large hail and damaging wind, some significant, were expected to continue along and ahead of the cold front into the night.

boundary_drivers: multi-layered cloud band over the eastern states|cold front/pre-frontal trough|Northeast urban corridor instability plume
day_narrative: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed from the Northeast into the Mid-Atlantic, with damaging wind gusts as the main hazard. A tornado or two and hail were possible in stronger bands, especially as storms approached the DC to New York corridor.

boundary_drivers: eastern slopes of New Mexico terrain|northwest flow over southern High Plains|southward-moving squall line
day_narrative: Storms developed along the southern Rockies and moved into eastern New Mexico and west Texas. Initial hail and isolated tornado potential transitioned toward a damaging-wind threat as storms organized into a line.

boundary_drivers: cold front across the northern/central Plains|shortwave trough in the northern Rockies|Missouri River corridor
day_narrative: Severe storms developed over Nebraska and South Dakota with potential for very large hail and severe wind gusts. Clusters later moved eastward toward the Missouri River, with the strongest gusts tied to organized convective segments.

boundary_drivers: ongoing clusters across IA/MO/WI/IL|shortwave trough into the Great Lakes|warm/moist corridor into northern Illinois and Wisconsin
day_narrative: Clusters of severe storms continued from the middle Missouri Valley into Wisconsin and Illinois, with tornado watches needed in southern Wisconsin and northern Illinois. Large hail, damaging wind, and a few tornadoes were all possible where storms interacted with the richer moisture corridor.

boundary_drivers: ejecting shortwave trough over SD/NE|residual outflow boundary across IN/OH|Kansas to Missouri instability corridor
day_narrative: Several severe clusters formed from the central Plains into the Midwest. Initial discrete storms posed large hail and isolated tornado potential, then western Kansas storms organized into an MCS with a mainly wind-driven threat farther southeast.

boundary_drivers: primary outflow boundary along the Red River|secondary outflow boundary across Oklahoma|dissipating nocturnal MCS
day_narrative: A dissipating nocturnal MCS left outflow boundaries across Oklahoma and north Texas, where strong recovery supported new severe development. Initial discrete storms posed very large hail and a brief tornado risk before upscale growth increased damaging-wind potential.

boundary_drivers: shortwave trough across Kansas/eastern Texas Panhandle|northwest Oklahoma/eastern Texas Panhandle MCS|Red River instability corridor
day_narrative: A southern Plains thunderstorm complex developed ahead of a shortwave trough and moved southeast through Oklahoma toward north Texas and western Arkansas. Strong to severe wind gusts were the primary concern, with hail also possible in stronger cores.

boundary_drivers: northwesterly flow into Wisconsin|western Lake Superior convective corridor|instability over the upper Great Lakes
storm_modes: severe storm cluster|bowing line|downstream line segments
day_narrative: Severe storms spread across Wisconsin and the upper Great Lakes in strengthening northwesterly flow. Damaging winds and large hail were the main threats, with a bowing line near Door County maintaining at least localized downstream severe potential.

boundary_drivers: Midwest to Ohio Valley instability gradient|weak outflow near upper Ohio River|southeast-moving squall lines
day_narrative: Scattered swaths of damaging wind and hail occurred from the Midwest into the Ohio Valley. Multiple clusters and squall lines propagated southeast, with the greatest severe signal west of the Appalachians.

boundary_drivers: warm-advection plume into the Upper Midwest|southern Minnesota instability corridor|nocturnal low-level jet
day_narrative: The Enhanced risk centered on the Upper Midwest, where storms were expected to develop near southern Minnesota and evolve overnight. Initial supercells favored very large hail and a tornado or two, then the threat transitioned to damaging wind as storms clustered.

boundary_drivers: Upper Mississippi Valley instability corridor|capped warm sector|overnight bowing line over Wisconsin
day_narrative: SPC backed off earlier expectations for a significant Minnesota cluster, but maintained an Enhanced risk for the Upper Mississippi Valley. Isolated supercells and later bowing-line evolution produced large hail, damaging wind, and limited tornado potential.

boundary_drivers: rapid east-southeast MCS across the Dakotas/Minnesota|warm front/instability gradient|secondary SD/NE storm corridor
day_narrative: Several bands of damaging winds, large hail, and isolated tornadoes were expected from eastern South Dakota into Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa, and northern Illinois. The main uncertainty was timing and placement of the most intense MCS corridors.

boundary_drivers: warm front from Iowa to Indiana|developing bow echo over north-central Minnesota|cold front across the Dakotas/Minnesota
day_narrative: A large cluster evolved from eastern Iowa into northern Illinois, southern Wisconsin, and Indiana near a warm front. Separate severe storms over the Dakotas/Minnesota included a developing bow echo, with damaging winds and hail the main hazards.

boundary_drivers: boundary from northern Nebraska into Minnesota|strong capping over the Upper Midwest|late-afternoon heating corridor
day_narrative: The Enhanced risk focused on the Upper Midwest, where strong capping delayed storm initiation until peak heating. If storms formed along the boundary, large hail, damaging wind, and a couple tornadic storms were possible.

boundary_drivers: central High Plains stationary front|Front Range initiation zone|southeast Colorado to Kansas/Oklahoma corridor
storm_modes: organized cluster|forward-propagating MCS|supercells merging into clusters
day_narrative: An organizing cluster across the central High Plains was expected to evolve into a forward-propagating MCS. Damaging wind was the main hazard, with large hail possible during the earlier supercell/cluster phase.

boundary_drivers: cold front from Iowa to Oklahoma|eastward-moving lines/clusters|effective boundary in Minnesota/Iowa
day_narrative: Scattered to numerous severe storms were expected from Iowa to Oklahoma, with large hail, damaging winds, and a couple tornadoes. Storms became more linear through evening, shifting the severe threat toward damaging winds along the I-44 corridor.

boundary_drivers: amplifying Great Lakes/Quebec shortwave|pre-frontal bands|pre-frontal outflow near I-40 secondary corridor
storm_modes: bands of strong/severe convection|QLCS segments|embedded rotating storms
day_narrative: Scattered to numerous swaths of damaging wind were expected from the Ohio Valley to New England, with tornado potential especially from northern Pennsylvania to northern New England. Bands of convection organized ahead of a strong shortwave and tracked east-northeast through evening.

boundary_drivers: remnant Harvey circulation/dry slot|Ark-La-Miss to western Alabama instability plume|broken tropical rainbands
storm_modes: tropical rainband cells|semi-discrete low-topped storms|broken linear segments
day_narrative: The remnant Harvey environment produced an Enhanced tornado risk from the Ark-La-Miss into western Alabama. Low-level shear and destabilization east of the dry slot supported short-lived tornadoes within broken bands and semi-discrete cells.

boundary_drivers: remnant circulation of tropical cyclone Harvey|bands over the Carolinas|cold front in northern Plains secondary region
day_narrative: Harvey's remnants supported severe bands across the Carolinas, with tornadoes and damaging wind gusts expected into evening. The strongest activity moved through central North Carolina and north-central South Carolina, while other areas had weaker instability or convergence.

boundary_drivers: southeastward-moving cold front|strong Great Lakes shortwave trough|lower Great Lakes/OH Valley instability corridor
day_narrative: A cold front and amplifying shortwave produced a damaging-wind corridor across the lower Great Lakes and Ohio Valley. A small 45 percent wind area was added where stronger flow and storm organization overlapped in northern Indiana and northwest Ohio.

boundary_drivers: Hurricane Irma outer rainbands|southeast Florida coastal instability|initial QLCS/outflow area
day_narrative: Irma's outer bands increasingly affected south and central Florida through the night. Tornado risk was greatest along the east coast where instability and enlarging low-level hodographs overlapped with semi-discrete rainband cells.

boundary_drivers: Hurricane Irma right-front quadrant|Florida Peninsula coastal instability|northward-shifting rainbands
storm_modes: small fast-moving tropical cells|semi-discrete rainband supercells|bands
day_narrative: Irma's tornado threat continued across much of the Florida Peninsula as the hurricane moved northward. Extreme low-level shear supported small, fast-moving rotating cells, with the greatest risk shifting north with the circulation.

boundary_drivers: pre-frontal line in eastern South Dakota|recent outflow boundary|western Minnesota instability corridor
day_narrative: A significant severe-storm corridor developed across the eastern Dakotas into western Minnesota. A pre-frontal line intersected a recent outflow boundary, supporting damaging winds, tornadoes, and large hail before weakening farther east.

boundary_drivers: lee trough/cold front|central High Plains moisture plume|northeast Colorado to Nebraska supercell corridor
day_narrative: Northeast Colorado, northwest Kansas, and Nebraska were the focus for long-track supercells. Very large hail was the primary hazard, with damaging wind and a few tornadoes possible as storms matured and moved east-southeast.

boundary_drivers: frontal zone across Kansas|Pacific cold front in the Texas Panhandle|central/southern Plains cold front
day_narrative: Severe storms spread across the central and southern Plains, with a maturing squall line over Kansas and additional development near a Pacific cold front in west Texas. Large hail and damaging winds were primary, with one or two tornadoes possible.

boundary_drivers: cold front from Missouri to Oklahoma|strong low-level warm advection|Illinois/Missouri pre-frontal corridor
day_narrative: A progressive trough and cold front produced severe storms from the south-central Plains to the upper Great Lakes. Damaging gusts, large hail, and a few tornadoes were possible, especially as storms spread across Missouri and Illinois during the evening.

boundary_drivers: east-southeastward moving cold front|dryline across Oklahoma/north Texas|I-35 corridor
day_narrative: Severe storms developed across the southern and central Plains along a cold front and dryline. Significant hail and a couple tornadoes were the early southern Plains concerns, transitioning toward severe wind as an accelerating line moved east.

boundary_drivers: southeastward-moving cold front|warm sector across IL/IN/OH|lower Great Lakes warm front corridor
day_narrative: Severe storms extended from the mid Mississippi Valley into the lower Great Lakes. Warm-sector supercells produced tornado potential early, then the primary risk transitioned toward damaging wind as a squall line advanced east into Ohio and Pennsylvania.

boundary_drivers: deepening surface low|warm front|eastward-advancing cold front|pre-frontal surface trough
day_narrative: A progressive shortwave and deepening surface cyclone focused severe storms from the Arklatex into the lower Mississippi and Ohio Valleys. Forecast soundings and MDs supported discrete supercells early, followed by an increasingly organized squall line with bowing segments. Damaging winds became the main hazard by evening, but tornado potential persisted near the warm frontal corridor and embedded circulations.

boundary_drivers: warm front across northern Alabama|remnant outflow boundary|elevated mixed-layer plume|weak surface low
storm_modes: discrete supercells|supercell clusters|MCS with embedded supercells|bows
day_narrative: The Moderate Risk centered on warm-front supercells across the Tennessee Valley and Southeast, where strong tornadoes and very large hail were expected.
